1f167d1277c4.title: Oxigraph multi-graph search for WHO IRIS
1f167d1277c4.content: Skill iris-oxigraph: How to build WHO IRIS catalogue and Qualified Dublin Core metadata into partitioned N-Quads, and query it with Oxigraph — in Bun on the build side, in WebAssembly in the browser — including cross-graph joins and facet counts. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation . The IRIS catalogue and its Dublin Core records are compiled into named graphs and queried with Oxigraph: natively in Bun at build time, and as WebAssembly in a browser. One SPARQL query can then join Dublin Core properties, catalogue containment and bitstream access gates — which DSpace Discovery cannot do in a single call.

ac9d09ce9206.title: Build and query
ac9d09ce9206.content: # Build from catalogue/nodes and site/dublin-core into dist/oxigraph/ bun run scripts/build-iris-oxigraph.ts # Build from exported DSpace records (the CDN release's records/ tree) bun run scripts/build-iris-oxigraph.ts --records <dir> --out <dir> # Load dist/oxigraph/who-iris-dataset.nq and run sample searches and facets bun run scripts/iris-oxigraph-search.ts bun test scripts/tests/iris-oxigraph.test.ts . scripts/iris-oxigraph-search.ts exports IrisOxigraphEngine (loadSpine, loadCommunity, searchSpine, complexSearch, facetCounts). The CDN exporter (scripts/iris-cdn/run.ts) calls the build over exported records and publishes each output file as graph/<file>.

dfd5d175b425.title: 1. Graphs and files
dfd5d175b425.content: The build writes, sorted and de-duplicated so unchanged inputs give byte-identical files: . | Tier 1, the spine — <https://iris.who.int/graph/spine>, in who-iris-spine.nq and .nq.gz. Hierarchy (dspace:Community, dspace:Collection), item Handles, titles, first creator, issued date, and bitstream descriptors with copyright verdicts. Loaded first. | Tier 2, one partition per community — <https://iris.who.int/graph/community/{id}>, in iris_who_int_graph_community_{id}.nq and .nq.gz. The full Dublin Core of that community’s items: MeSH authorities, abstracts, spatial coverage, govdoc numbers, ISBNs. Mounted on demand. | Catalogue and metadata graphs — <https://iris.who.int/graph/catalogue> and <https://iris.who.int/graph/metadata>, each in its own iris_who_int_graph_{catalogue,metadata}.nq(.gz), and merged in who-iris-dataset.nq and .nq.gz for server-side use and integrity checks. | subgraph-manifest.json — the spine and each community partition, with file names, quad counts and item counts. | queries.json — prepared SPARQL queries. | . Namespaces . | dspace: = https://iris.who.int/ns/dspace# — catalogue terms (Item, inCommunity, hasBitstream, fileName, …). | dspaceNs: = https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant-core/v0/ns/dspace/ — Dublin Core value terms, including authority. | . No binary bytes in the graph . PDFs, cover images and archives are never stored as literals. A bitstream node carries only: . | dspace:fileName (e.g. "WPR-RDO-2020-003-eng.pdf") | dspace:mediaType (e.g. "application/pdf") | dspace:fileBytes (integer) | dspace:copyrightGate — the copyright gate’s verdict, e.g. "permitted" | . The bytes are fetched from the CDN.

6e2391a33d5b.title: 2. Requirements
6e2391a33d5b.content: | # | Requirement | Why, in one line | . | OX-1 | Mint stable URIs at the extractor (https://iris.who.int/entity/item/{handle}#{prop}_{idx}); the build fails if any blank node remains | no multi-document collisions, every node addressable, no normalizer pass | . | OX-2 | Store zero binary bytes in RDF | keeps WASM memory small; binaries are static files on the CDN | . | OX-3 | Join across named graphs with explicit GRAPH blocks | separates containment and rights from bibliographic description | . | OX-4 | Use Handle URIs as the item subject (https://hdl.handle.net/...) | identity resolves outside WHO’s servers | . | OX-5 | Treat bitstream rights as access gates | results can be filtered by whether the PDF may be downloaded | . | OX-6 | Partition by community | a client fetches only the slice it needs | . | OX-7 | Never scan whole-corpus text in SPARQL | full text belongs in a static inverted index | . | OX-8 | Preserve controlled-vocabulary authorities (dspaceNs:authority) | distinguishes MeSH headings from free keywords | . | OX-9 | Append-only streaming partition emission | bounded memory at 300,000 items. Not met yet: buildIrisDataset holds and sorts every quad in memory; StreamingPartitionWriter is defined but unused | .

a87afd36be06.title: 3. SPARQL recipes
a87afd36be06.content: Recipe 1: multi-condition search . Items in the Western Pacific community, issued in or after 2000, with a subject containing “guidelines”, and a PDF whose copyright verdict is permitted. PREFIX dcterms: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> PREFIX dspace: <https://iris.who.int/ns/dspace#> PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> PREFIX rdf: <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#> PREFIX xsd: <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#> SELECT DISTINCT ?handle ?title ?creator ?issued ?pdfName WHERE { # 1. Join Dublin Core Metadata GRAPH <https://iris.who.int/graph/metadata> { ?handle dcterms:title ?title ; dcterms:creator ?crNode ; dcterms:subject ?sNode . ?crNode rdf:value ?creator . ?sNode rdf:value ?subject . OPTIONAL { ?handle dcterms:issued ?issued } } # 2. Join Catalogue Hierarchy & Access Gates GRAPH <https://iris.who.int/graph/catalogue> { ?handle dspace:inCommunity ?comm ; dspace:hasBitstream ?bs . ?comm rdfs:label ?commLabel . ?bs dspace:mediaType "application/pdf" ; dspace:fileName ?pdfName ; dspace:copyrightGate "permitted" . } # 3. Multi-Field Filter Evaluation BIND(IF(BOUND(?issued), xsd:integer(SUBSTR(STR(?issued), 1, 4)), 0) AS ?year) FILTER ( CONTAINS(LCASE(?subject), "guidelines") && CONTAINS(LCASE(?commLabel), "western pacific") && (?year >= 2000) ) } ORDER BY DESC(?year) . Recipe 2: facet counts . Item counts per subject term and its authority. PREFIX dcterms: <http://purl.org/dc/terms/> PREFIX rdf: <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#> PREFIX dspaceNs: <https://litlfred.github.io/folio-assistant-core/v0/ns/dspace/> SELECT ?subject (COUNT(DISTINCT ?handle) AS ?itemCount) ?authority WHERE { GRAPH <https://iris.who.int/graph/metadata> { ?handle dcterms:subject ?sNode . ?sNode rdf:value ?subject . OPTIONAL { ?sNode dspaceNs:authority ?authority } } } GROUP BY ?subject ?authority ORDER BY DESC(?itemCount) ?subject .

0765e8907150.title: 4. Browser pattern: spine first, communities on demand
0765e8907150.content: import oxigraph from 'oxigraph'; // Where the graph files are served from, e.g. a release's graph/ directory. const BASE = '<graph-base-url>'; async function gunzipText(resp: Response): Promise<string> { const stream = resp.body!.pipeThrough(new DecompressionStream('gzip')); return new Response(stream).text(); } const store = new oxigraph.Store(); // 1. Fetch the spine and the manifest const [spineResp, manifestResp] = await Promise.all([ fetch(`${BASE}/who-iris-spine.nq.gz`), fetch(`${BASE}/subgraph-manifest.json`), ]); const manifest = await manifestResp.json(); // 2. Load the spine: hierarchy, title search and rights filtering work now store.load(await gunzipText(spineResp), { format: 'application/n-quads' }); // 3. Mount a community when the user selects it. load() adds its named // graph without clobbering what is already in the store. async function mountCommunity(commId: string) { const partition = manifest.tiers.tier2_communities.partitions[commId]; if (!partition) return; const resp = await fetch(`${BASE}/${partition.fileGz}`); store.load(await gunzipText(resp), { format: 'application/n-quads' }); } // 4. Run a prepared query locally for (const binding of store.query(myPreparedQuery)) { console.log(binding.get('title').value); } .

dde2002f4056.title: Reading IRIS changes over DSpace REST
dde2002f4056.content: Skill iris-rest-feed: How to read changes from the WHO IRIS DSpace 7 REST API: the nightly “changed since” walk over Discovery, the weekly reconciliation that stands in for the deletions REST does not report, and the guard that stops a short listing from reading as a mass withdrawal. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation . Changes are read from the DSpace REST API only. REST has no change feed with deletions, so a nightly walk is paired with a weekly reconciliation. The code is scripts/iris-cdn/rest-feed.ts; its tests run on fixtures in scripts/tests/iris-cdn.test.ts.

c6cbdde13038.title: What live IRIS accepts
c6cbdde13038.content: . | Discovery offers only five sortOptions: score, dc.title, dc.date.issued, dc.date.accessioned, dc.date.available. sort=lastModified,DESC returns HTTP 422. | Changes are found with a Solr range query instead: query=lastModified:[<isoZ> TO *]. | The bound must be a Z-suffixed UTC timestamp. A +00:00 offset returns totalElements: 0. | .

ade002335732.title: Endpoints
ade002335732.content: | Use | Request | . | Changed items since cursor | GET /server/api/discover/search/objects?dsoType=ITEM&query=lastModified:[{isoZ} TO *]&sort=dc.date.accessioned,DESC&page=N&size=100 | . | Weekly full item listing | GET /server/api/discover/search/objects?dsoType=ITEM&sort=dc.date.accessioned,DESC&page=N&size=100 | . | Collection-scoped batch (initial load) | GET /server/api/discover/search/objects?dsoType=ITEM&scope={collectionUuid}&sort=dc.date.accessioned,DESC&page=N&size=100 | . | Communities / collections with parent | GET /server/api/core/{communities|collections}?page=N&size=100&embed=parentCommunity | . | One item with its files and collection | GET /server/api/core/items/{uuid}?embed=bundles/bitstreams&embed=owningCollection | . | Bundle bitstreams beyond page 0 | GET /server/api/core/bundles/{bundleUuid}/bitstreams?page=N&size=100 | . | A file’s bytes | GET /server/api/core/bitstreams/{uuid}/content | .

e8c800deb78f.title: Nightly: changedSince(cursor)
e8c800deb78f.content: . | Normalise cursor to UTC Z (new Date(Date.parse(cursor)).toISOString()) and run the range query above. | Page through the matching result set. | The cursor is inclusive: an item modified at that instant is read again, not missed. Re-reading an unchanged item writes the same bytes. | Return the items oldest first, de-duplicated by UUID. | . The cursor is the newest lastModified read, kept in state/cursor.json. A failed night does not advance it.

6c59cc81d878.title: Metadata changes without the PDF changing
6c59cc81d878.content: A PDF may stay the same while its Dublin Core changes. Records and files are handled separately: . | A record is re-read whenever its item appears in the walk. A PDF is re-fetched only if its DSpace MD5 changed. | Communities and collections are re-read in full every night (allContainers). A renamed collection changes no item, and DSpace 7 does not expose lastModified for these. An unchanged one serializes to the same bytes. | The weekly metadata check. The weekly listing pages carry each item’s metadata. metadataSha hashes it canonically, and any item whose hash differs from the one last ingested is re-read. That catches edits that did not move lastModified, without one fetch per item. | .

4319aa607d3c.title: Weekly: allItems and withdrawnOrHidden
4319aa607d3c.content: . | List every item ID Discovery returns. | Compare that list with the IDs the library holds. | Guard. If more than 1% of held items are missing, the listing is treated as faulty and nothing is marked. Possible causes are a paging fault, an outage or a Solr reindex. | Re-fetch each missing item by ID. Mark it withdrawn only if IRIS confirms it: withdrawn: true, or a 404 (gone), 401 or 403 (private). | .

1edb17ddc77e.title: Fixity
1edb17ddc77e.content: DSpace reports an MD5 checkSum for each bitstream. Downloaded bytes must match it before their SHA-256 is recorded. A mismatch quarantines the bitstream and reports it. It is never retried silently.

07cf80ae9d21.title: Politeness
07cf80ae9d21.content: Requests are made one at a time, with a User-Agent that names the project and its repository, and back off on 429 and 503. The initial load is paced to the budget stated in Task_StateBudget (processes/iris-cdn-initial-load.bpmn), including maxRequestsPerSecond.

13aef361e8d5.title: A subset by reference: run.ts subset
13aef361e8d5.content: bun scripts/iris-cdn/run.ts subset catalogues part of IRIS without fetching any bytes (who-iris#207): for each item, the Dublin Core record as DSpace returns it and a referenced catalogue node whose ORIGINAL bitstreams link to https://iris.who.int/bitstreams/{uuid}/download. The subsets it reads live in scripts/iris-cdn/subsets/. | Which items. A handles file goes first (for example the IRIS items a DAK cites), then a Discovery query. The query is a field query on metadata (dc.title, dc.subject, dc.subject.mesh, dc.description.abstract), not a bare keyword. A bare keyword also searches the PDF text, so vaccine matches a report that mentions one in passing. | Write boolean operators in capitals. Solr reads a lowercase or as a word: HIV or immunization or vaccine matches fewer items than vaccine alone. | A Handle to an item: GET /server/api/pid/find?id=hdl:{handle} answers 302 to /server/api/core/items/{uuid}. | An ISBN or govdoc to an item: query=dc.identifier.isbn:"{isbn13}" or query=dc.identifier.govdoc:"WHO/HIV/2017.09". | A sample is one-row pages at seeded random offsets, so the same seed gives the same items. | No fixity is claimed. IRIS reports an MD5. A sha256 is recorded only once the bytes are fetched (R13), so the MD5 goes in the bitstream’s note. | Hand-made nodes win. An item whose Handle or UUID another node already carries is skipped and reported. The tool rewrites only its own nodes, the ones whose note starts “Catalogued by reference by scripts/iris-cdn/run.ts subset”, and only when they changed. | A token, when IRIS gives one, comes from the IRIS_DSPACE_TOKEN environment variable as Authorization: Bearer …. It never appears in an argument, a file or a log. | .

f8afb211bf9d.title: Knowledge Graph separation — the method
f8afb211bf9d.content: Skill kg-separation: Separate a Knowledge Graph into its own repository — as a CONTENT repository (files to read, no code) and a TOOLS repository (the code that writes and checks it) — once it is too large, or its consumers or cadence differ. The end-to-end method: the signals that trigger it, the preconditions, eleven stages each with the command that gates it, the owner’s decision points, how identifiers, QA and publication move, how the parent consumes the result, rollback, and the post-move sweep that a move between the pair owes before the parent re-pins. graph-detanglement owns stages 1–3; this skill owns the rest. Bootstrap + bootstrap-tools and cat-harness + the tools layer are the worked examples. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . Skill id: kg-separation · Package: graph-management Process: kg-separation.bpmn . This is the replicable method for separating a Knowledge Graph that is too large to handle, or whose consumers differ, written from what the bootstrap separation did. graph-detanglement is the practice for stages 1–3 (declare in place, detangle, isolate). Read it for those; this skill points to it and does not restate it. Everything from “split the tools out” to “the parent’s copy is deleted” is here.

4df41e768290.title: When — the signals, and none of them alone
4df41e768290.content: Separate when the graph is too large to handle, or when a business reason separates it: “split only where consumers or cadences differ”. Size is often not the reason — bootstrap is 33 files and left because its readers and its release cadence differ from cat-harness’s. Record the signals in the work item before deciding: . | signal | how it is measured | . | files and bytes per layer | git ls-files \| cut -d/ -f1 \| sort \| uniq -c | . | clone cost | bun run cat health → repository-size | . | gate time a content change pays | bun run cat gates (the gate count and wall time) | . | merge contention | commits per day on main; PRs re-conflicted before merge | . | cohesion and cut of the candidate | bun run cat kg:detangle | . | wrong-direction edges within one layer — modules bucketed into the proposed repos by path rule | check:partition (its root is ONE layer; read the scope it prints) | . | wrong-direction edges between layers — checked against each one’s declared needs | bun run cat kg:detangle:direction, blocking in CI | . | wrong-direction references — the prose axis, not the import axis | check:reference-direction | . | what the tools would drag along | the import cone of the would-be tools package (check:tools-closure once it exists) | .

68ddafb88d2b.title: An example pointing up is a mention, not a dependency
68ddafb88d2b.content: check:reference-direction holds that nothing names a layer that depends on it. One kind of pointer does not break that rule: a lower layer citing a source as an example, where the one copy of that source lives in a layer above it. For example, a base IG layer’s document kind and voice quote a draft reference architecture whose library entry belongs to a folio above it; two copies of one key break the bibliography build, so: . | One copy. The source’s library entry lives only in the layer that owns it. The lower layer deletes its copy and never re-ingests it. | The lower layer keeps a pointer. A document-kind source’s ref is a URL to the owner’s published library page (DocumentKindSourceSchema allows “a library entry id or a URL”). A voice source names the owning repository in instance and adds its url. A quote keeps its libraryId and sectionId. | It is checked where the copy is. The lower layer cannot read the sections, so its quote check reports such a quote as “an example held by , not checked here". That is not a pass and not a failure (https://github.com/litlfred/smart-base/blob/main/scripts/gen-dth-term-findings.ts, `EXAMPLE_POINTERS`). | It is a mention. The lower layer’s build does not need the higher layer, and nothing it runs reads through the pointer. The URL form is already an address under check:reference-direction’s URL exemption (“a location is where a thing is, not a dependency on it”). A pointer that something would need to resolve in order to build is a dependency, and the content moves up instead. | .

d7b5ddcdaea3.title: Preconditions
d7b5ddcdaea3.content: . | Names agree before the cut — directory, declared name, package name. A rename after the cut is a cross-repository change. | One directory per layer, so extraction is one move, not a sift. | Every gate that guards the boundary has been watched failing — plant a violation, see it red, remove it. A boundary gate can pass while guarding nothing: unable to fail, blind to side-effect imports, or blind across layers. | The owner’s decisions are recorded in the work item (the list below). | “Generated output is the contract” is written down: what crosses the boundary is the generated file, and any tool may produce it. | .

5dc8b916a329.title: The pair: a content repository and a tools repository
5dc8b916a329.content: A separated Knowledge Graph is two repositories, not one. |   | content (<name>) | tools (<name>-tools) | . | holds | files to read — .md, .json, .bpmn, generated schemas, READMEs, diagrams | the code that writes and checks the content — Zod sources, generators, README/diagram writers, content checks | . | code | none (FR-7 — a reader needs nothing installed) | yes, with a declared, minimal dependency set | . | depends on | nothing | the content, and nothing above it — check:tools-closure | . | is used by | the parent harness, pinned | the content’s own checks, and the parent (a package) | . The rules of the pattern: . | The Zod source moves DOWN into the tools repository — not up into the harness. Zod in the harness makes a content release wait on the harness, which itself needs the content: a cycle. | The tools repository owns the content checks AND the README and diagram writers — one copy, which the parent harness also calls. It is not a second harness: a content Knowledge Graph declares no visualisers. It is one toolset over swappable content, so a different visualiser is a different toolset. | Every tool is a script an agent runs as the actor in a process step. Agentic first. A GitHub Actions workflow may be described, but ships disabled, and nothing that costs money runs unless the owner asks. | Harness output ABOUT the content stays with the harness (hosted): its QA verdicts (kgQaHomeFor), translation templates (translationsHomeFor), exported graph and glossary ledger. The content repository carries only what its own checks need. | . Staged content with no tools repository yet — the finding, not the silence . A layer can be planned as a content repository before its -tools pair is authorised. Declare it — separation: "content" in <name>.json; the content half of an existing pair is read from the tools layer’s supports and needs nothing — and kg:audit’s content-instance-holds-code records a finding naming every code file still inside it. It is a minor QA warning, not a failure, because the tolerated set is small; a warning still names each file, so the violation is never silent. The remedy splits by what the code is: generic code (it works for any instance of its kind — any DSpace catalogue, any PDF) moves into the platform and takes the layer root as an argument; layer-specific code waits for <name>-tools.

d9a43037a59c.title: The stages
d9a43037a59c.content: Each stage names its lane (a role in scenarios/roles.json) and the command that gates it. A stage is done when its gate is green, never when the work looks finished. | # | stage | lane | gate | . | 0 | Brief, measure the signals, claim | authoring-agent | signals in the work item; bun run cat beans:claim <id> | . | 1–3 | Declare in place, detangle, isolate | authoring-agent | graph-detanglement — all its gates | . | 4 | Identity: name, version, iriBase, needs, nodeSchemas in the declaration; move the base once | platform-authoring-agent | iri:sync -- --from <old base> then iri:sync:check; check:node-iris | . | 5 | Hosted outputs out of the content | platform-authoring-agent | the content leak test’s pending list is empty | . | 6 | Split content from tools: create <name>-tools/ as a sibling, move the code, cut its import cone | platform-authoring-agent | FR-7 (content holds no code); check:tools-closure; generated files byte-identical before and after | . | 7 | Publication plan: every identifier the content mints is a file some step publishes, at /v<major>/ | publication-manager | check:node-iris; the site layout in instance-publication §”The release site” | . | 8 | Rehearse standalone: copy content + tools alone into a temporary directory and run the tools’ checks there | build-pipeline | green with nothing else on the path; an empty tree exits non-zero | . | 9 | Authorise — report what moves, sizes, what breaks, and wait | administrator | the owner’s answer (deletion-requires-confirmation) | . | 10 | Seed: the owner creates the repositories; once the source has settled, seed main, then the content and tools as reviewed PRs, with history | administrator, then authoring-agent | bun run cat seed:ready --layer <name> --rehearse answers settled for each layer, at seed time; then the seeding PRs reviewed and green | . | 11 | Parent consumes, additively: pin (a SHA while staging, a version once released), repoint imports, keep the parent’s copy. After any move of files between the pair, run the post-move sweep first (below) | platform-authoring-agent | the parent green with the dependency declared; check:published-refs; every gate in the sweep table | . | 12 | First release: tag, publish /v<major>/ | publication-manager | check:version-bump; every identifier dereferences (publish-verification (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)) | . | 13 | Cutover: the one commit retiring the parent’s copy into fsh-guts as a verified archive (the deposit state:seed --cutover makes: it must extract to the exact tree removed, with a provenance note), deposited into the PARENT’s fsh-guts before the removal, frozen, never refreshed or rendered: a relocation, not a deletion (sub-kg-lifecycle stage 13 has the steps) | administrator | only after 11 and 12 are green; DONE only when bun run cat separation:cutover:check --site, run in the separated repository, exits 0 (Tool separation-cutover-check: mounts, declarations resolve, no monorepo wiring, layer direction, the site builds from the mounts alone) | . | 14 | Independent refinement: each new release adopted by the parent as a reviewed step | authoring-agent | upstream-version-adoption | . Nothing is committed to the new repositories before stage 10, and stage 10 starts only when the owner says so. Until then the pair is staged as sibling directories in the parent (bootstrap/, bootstrap-tools/). Ready to seed? — asked at seed time, not at rehearsal . A seed is a snapshot: one commit that names the source sha, with no history. Every open PR whose diff touches the layer when the snapshot is taken is orphaned into the monorepo: after cutover its change is in neither the seed nor anywhere that reads it. Stage 8 asked whether the layer stands alone, but the tree has moved since. So GW_SeedReady sits between creating the repositories and seeding them, and asks again: . bun run cat seed:ready --layer cat-harness --rehearse --text # exit 0 settled, 1 not yet, 2 unknown . | criterion | not yet when | . | heavy movers | an open PR labelled heavy-mover touches the layer or the next one up | . | next layer | any open PR touches the next layer up, which imports this one | . | layer load | more than five open PRs touch the layer | . | moves | an open PR deletes a file in the layer, or renames one into or out of it. A generator’s own names do not count: an owned-tree path in merge-conflict-patterns.ts (content-hashed payloads, rail data) is renamed by every regen, so moving one changes what no seeded path means | . | standalone | bun test is red with only the layer and what it needs beside it, as sibling directories | . | upward paths | a path DECLARED in the layer — a Tool module, a QA criterion source, a render target — resolves only in a layer above it, so it breaks the day the layer stands alone | . A test about the WHOLE CHECKOUT lives at the top. A test that reads several sibling layers at once, or the aggregate root itself (.github/, .gitignore, the root declaration, beans/, todos/, memory/, fsh-guts/), is red in every layer it is placed in, so it goes in the root layer’s DECLARED test home — folio-assistant-tests in folio-assistant.json, at test/ — never in a layer and never at a path a runner hardcodes. Whatever names every layer belongs at the top, so each layer below stays standalone-green. Split a file when only some of its tests read the checkout, keep the fixture tests with their layer, compose the moved paths from ORIGIN_DIR (the directory the test was written in), and move a corpus describe whole when it carries a vacuity guard: a sibling left behind passes standalone over nothing. A test reading an UPPER layer’s files moves to that layer. It is red standing alone for the same reason, one level down: the file it reads is not in its layer’s closure. It goes in the upper layer’s DECLARED test home, which may import the lower layer — never the reverse — and it is split, pointed back to and composed from ORIGIN_DIR exactly as above. Check first that the file it reads really IS the upper layer’s: a path written from the checkout root (cat-harness/src/… read relative to the working directory) is red standing alone over a file the layer does hold, and the fix there is to resolve it from the test file, not to move it. A test that reads the checkout’s GIT asks which of two things it is. A standalone layer is a fresh clone with no origin and one commit, so a test handed this checkout’s remote, HEAD or origin/main fails there on a missing input. A test of LOGIC that merely reads git — address derivation, an upload URL’s shape, a commit IRI, resolving a short sha — builds a throwaway repository whose facts it sets (gitFixtureRepo in cat-harness’s test/support/git-fixture.ts) and passes that root, with every assertion exactly as strict; a function that resolves its root internally gains an optional root parameter defaulting to today’s. A check that THIS repository is configured right — its own Pages address, its committed pages’ banners — keeps its assertion verbatim and moves to the top-level test home above. upward paths counts what breaks, not what is out of sight. It counts declared paths that resolve above the layer, not dependents discovery cannot find: discovery is checkout-local on purpose, so a count of what it cannot see never reaches zero, and the risk is paths, not layers. A seeding pair is not upward. A higher layer’s Tool nodes may resolve into their implementer below through needs; the two are seeded in the same step, so none of those paths can break on seeding day. The HIGHER layer says so, seedsWith: [<lower>] in its declaration, because a lower layer naming one above it is the wrong direction. seed:ready states such paths in its note and does not count them; a path into any other layer above still counts. Four things to keep straight: . | The layer map is read off the declarations: livesAt.path is the directory, the longest needs chain is the depth, and the next layer is every layer one level up that needs this one. Nothing in the tool names a directory. | Every threshold is in the decision table, processes/kg/decisions/seed-readiness-gate.dmn. The script works out each criterion’s verdict by evaluating the table with the other facts at zero, so changing “five” is a one-line edit to the table. | heavy-mover is a label a person applies. With none on the layer, the criterion passes. If the label cannot be read, the answer is could-not-determine. | The rehearsal runs only on request, with --rehearse. It copies the layer and its needs into a scratch workspace (~150 MB and ~8,000 tests for cat-harness) and refuses to start with less than 3 GB free. Without --rehearse, the standalone criterion is could-not-determine, so seed:ready cannot answer settled until a rehearsal has run. That consequence is the one constant SETTLED_REQUIRES_REHEARSAL. | . Could-not-determine is never clean. GitHub lists at most 3,000 files per PR, so a criterion that the unseen files could change is undetermined, and the gateway answers unknown and stops. An unknown only withholds settled, though. It never hides a finding that is already certain, so the table tests the not yet rows first. not yet goes to Drain: land, close or re-target the PRs it named, then ask again. The tool only reports. It never seeds, labels or comments.

aa1e908eabf5.title: The owner’s decisions
aa1e908eabf5.content: An agent asks these; it does not settle them. | Separate at all, and where the boundary is — after the signals are measured. | The address base for the extracted graph’s identifiers: under the parent, or the new repository’s own. | Where verdicts about it live: hosted in the harness, or in the content. | What the tools repository owns, and how its checks run (agent, package, described workflow). | Authorise the extraction (stage 9). | Whether the first release is a draft with a tag, or the first formal publication (instance-publication). | The cutover (stage 13). | .

5aea13619a63.title: Identifiers and versions
5aea13619a63.content: One iriBase and one version in the declaration. Identifiers a program reads and pages a person reads are both <iriBase>v<major>/…; the exact release is the pin’s (bootstrap-tools/schemas/release-iri.ts). A base move is bun run iri:sync -- --from <old base>, once. A $schema tag carries its schema’s own semver. The exported graph’s own @id moves only when the new repository actually publishes. A published node’s identifier must be its file’s path (check:node-iris).

de9e74a3df7d.title: Versions of the pair — same scheme, same start, then independent
de9e74a3df7d.content: . | At the split, both start at the content’s current version, for simplicity — bootstrap was 0.1.0, so bootstrap-tools starts at 0.1.0. | After that each is versioned on its own, by the same rules: semver, the bump computed from the exported surface (check:version-bump). | Tags are plain v<major>.<minor>.<patch> in each new repository: a standalone repository holds one layer, declared at its root, so the tag needs no name. check:version-bump reads the plain form only there; a repository of several layers — the parent while the pair is staged — keeps <name>-v<major>.<minor>.<patch>, because a plain tag could not say which layer it released. | A tools release says which content versions it handles as a list of supported MAJOR versions (bootstrap: [0]), never a range expression — instance-versioning rule 2 forbids range syntax, and within one major a newer minor or patch only adds (tagCompatible). A tool asked to work on a content major it does not list refuses rather than guesses. | .

f90ed7aaff65.title: How the parent consumes the pair
f90ed7aaff65.content: No git submodules, ever (remote-mount.md). | mechanism | when | details | . | Remote mount (remoteMounts) | staging & development | A declared directory fetched at a pinned 40-character SHA with a committed lock (index.lock.json) and consent record. Downstream checkout .gitignore automatically ignores mounted directory trees. | . | NPM KG retrieval (kg-retrieve-npm) | packaged distribution | package.json declared in <instance>.json (role: "package-manifest"). Tarball packed via pack-tarball with a folio-binary-release/v1 integrity record, downloadable via npm install or GitHub binary releases (unhydrated source vs hydrated store). | . | Package import | published tools | The parent imports the tools’ Zod schemas and pipeline writers as an npm package dependency. | . | Upstream pins | maintenance | upstream-pins.json, maintained by upstream-version-adoption.bpmn. | . Separation lessons . | Downstream Gitignore Contract: When remote mounts populate a layer directory in the consumer repository, the consumer’s .gitignore must ignore the mounted paths. Otherwise, git treats external files as uncommitted local files. index.config.json automatically includes all remoteMounts paths in the generated .gitignore. | Folded Layer Aliases: When a layer or subgraph is folded into another (e.g. cat-openapi folded into cat-harness as named subgraph openapi), external forks or dependencies may still carry needs: ["cat-openapi"]. schemas/kg/harness-config.ts maintains FOLDED_INSTANCE_ALIASES to resolve these. | Asset Permission & License Validation: Pre-separation audits must verify library/withheld.json and copyright gates. Materializing or mounting a separated catalogue without verified asset clearance causes 404s and broken links on published documentation. | NPM Manifest in the KG: package.json is an authored pre-packaging asset in the Knowledge Graph (role: "package-manifest"), and .tgz release tarballs are tracked as folio-binary-release/v1 state documents with SHA-256 integrity digests. | No Relative Directory Climbing Across Repositories: Once separated into standalone checkouts, climbing ../.. escapes the repository boundary into .claude/worktrees/ or the parent filesystem and fails with Cannot find module. All cross-repository imports MUST be authored as package imports (e.g. @litlfred/cat-harness/... or via package exports), or resolved through package specifiers / tsconfig paths, NEVER through escaping filesystem ../.. traversals. | No Fixed-Depth Repository Root Assumptions (REPO): const REPO = resolve(import.meta.dir, "..", "..") points at the checkout root in a monorepo and above it in a standalone repository, so the script cannot find <instance>.json or scans sibling worktrees. Resolve the root dynamically — search upward for <instance>.json, index.config.json, or .git. | Clean Standalone Manifest (package.json) and Tooling Scaffolding: When extracting a layer to an upstream repository, package.json must be normalized: . | Operational commands must live under "scripts", not leftover monorepo "checkoutScripts". | Script definitions must NOT hardcode monorepo subdirectory paths (e.g. "bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/..." -> "bun run scripts/..."). | A standalone tsconfig.json must be present to prevent tsc from walking up to the monorepo root. | Explicit dependencies and devDependencies must be declared. | . | Fan-Out Recursion Guard in declaringInstances: When a mounted dependency carries its own nested remoteMounts, consumer remote fan-out must not mount sub-layers into roots that are already locked mounts of the parent checkout (!lockedMountPaths(checkout).has(rel)). Otherwise remoteFanOut mutates the child checkout’s tree and treeDigest verification fails. | Relative Directory Symlink Handling in Staging & Tarball Scripts: Recursive copies (cpSync(..., { recursive: true })) of trees with internal symlinked directories can recurse forever. Staging, site compilation, and packaging scripts must copy symlinks with { dereference: false } or use archive utilities (such as tar or rsync -a) that preserve symlink references. | Purely Declarative Ontologies vs. Companion Toolsets (FR-7): Purely declarative base repositories (such as litlfred/bootstrap) contain zero runtime execution code, zero test suites, and zero package.json manifests (FR-7). All graph compilation (JSON-LD export, BPMN diagram rendering, site staging, and schema validation) is executed by the companion tooling repository (bootstrap-tools). The declarative repository marks its render exemption (renderExemption: true) in its root manifest, and tooling scripts accept an explicit target repository argument (--repo <dir>). | Toolchain Decentralization (package.json, tsconfig.json, bunfig.toml): Tools and harness subgraphs must possess full standalone toolchain autonomy. package.json must be a standalone package manifest (e.g. @litlfred/<tools-layer>), bunfig.toml defines test preloads per layer, and tsconfig.json must set "noEmit": true and omit rootDir/outDir to prevent error TS6059: File is not under rootDir when cross-subgraph schemas or utilities are imported. See bun-use. | Monorepo Coordinator Demotion: Once tools and code are extracted to their respective packages, the root package.json is demoted to a private coordinator ("private": true) with narrowed tsconfig.json (test/**/*.ts). The root platform coordinates development workspaces, mounts, and integration tests, but never directly exports or publishes tool implementations. | Ephemeral File Purging and Root Hygiene: Ephemeral generated directories (_kg/, build/, test-results/) must NEVER be committed to the root repository or left unignored. Build outputs belong to the tool that produces them. | Layer Memory Preservation: Root directories beans/, todos/, and fsh-guts/ are the layer’s own durable working memory (the agent’s plan, the user’s todo queue, and the archival store). They are never overlaid across layers, never extracted to downstream packages, and stay at root by design. | A cutover is not done until the layer has re-pointed and can publish itself: livesAt is not a comment — remote-mount.ts takes livesAt.path as the mount path and seed-ready reads it as “still staged”. A path that was only ever a mount inside the parent’s site build serves nothing on its own, and generated pages keep absolute links to the parent’s paths, which 404 once the bytes move. Before stage 13: livesAt is gone, iriBase is declared, and the layer’s own site builds from its own repository. | The replayer must never live inside a layer it replays: if every workflow (and every downstream folio’s staging build, through a reusable workflow) bootstraps by running a script inside the directory being retired, the cutover breaks the first step of every job. Before stage 13, grep every workflow the parent ships for paths into the directory being retired, and give the parent a bootstrap entry point that lives in the parent and needs nothing mounted (a dependency-free .github/mount-from-lock.sh that fetches the pinned replayer). | A downstream’s CI is part of “green” for a cutover: a reusable workflow called @main (uses: litlfred/folio-assistant/.github/workflows/folio-staging.yml@main) runs the PARENT’s current workflow in the DOWNSTREAM’s repository. A cutover that is green in the parent can therefore be red in every folio at once, and the red lands on whatever pull request the folio author opens next — it reads as their failure. Stage 12’s “green” includes one dispatched staging run of at least one downstream folio after the cutover commit. | A separated checkout must run its own tests and type-check its own subgraphs: run them in a fresh standalone clone. A test that reads <checkout>/../package.json fails with ENOENT outside the composed tree (lesson 6 by another route), and a tsconfig.json whose include omits named subgraphs (openapi/, archimate/) is green while never reading them. A test or type-check that silently depends on the composition, or silently skips part of the repository, is not evidence the separated repository works. | The kinds a declaration is judged against come from the checkout being read, not from where the harness module sits: the graph-typology registry reads the checkout under inspection first (defaultTypologyRoots; $REPO_ROOT still overrides), then its own; a kind both declare is shadowed and reported, never merged. Otherwise two layouts give two answers about one correct declaration. Every path a declaration names is resolved in one run by check:declaration-resolution, and separation:cutover:check uses it as its declarations condition. | .

2acfaa64288c.title: After a move lands — the post-move sweep
2acfaa64288c.content: Moving files between the pair is one reviewed commit in each repository; making the repositories that consume the move work again is most of the work. Run the sweep after a move lands and before the parent re-pins (stage 11), and do not call the move done until every gate in this table is green in a composed checkout at the matched pins. When another layer links into the moved path, declare the move first, so the layers can re-pin in any order: two-phase-move. | what still names the old home | the gate that catches it | the fix | . | A Tool node’s invoke.shell | kg:audit criterion tool-invoke-path-resolves (CRITICAL) | rewrite the invokes in each tools/<id>/<id>.json | . | Prose and commands in skills, guides, READMEs, BPMN documentation, workflows | check:command-paths | the rewrite rule below | . | A script’s own usage string | check:usage-paths | rewrite it in the receiving layer | . | Printed and RUN commands: “Run: …” remedies, generated banners, shell hooks, an e2e global setup | check:published-instance-exports, check:invocation-parity, security:gate (all three match paths by text), and the unit tests | rewrite the strings in the receiving layer | . | A wrapper generator’s list of the scripts it wraps | bat:sync / bat:sync:check (the writer errors on the first missing file) | update the list | . | Partition rules naming moved files | check:partition (“exact rule(s) name a file that is not in …”) | remove the dead rules | . | A kind-validator node pointing at a moved module | check:kind-validators:require-all | open: how a node in one layer names a module in the other | . | A writer’s claims in qa-refresh: files the writer used to rewrite became output it writes | qa:refresh (“N file(s) no declared writer claims”) | update the writer’s claims | . | A visualiser route a generator computed by hand | uml:overview inside skill:register (“no glossary page at …”) | use the declared route (declaredRoute(<core>, "glossary-page")) | . | A browser bundle importing a node-only module through a package import | navbar:assets (“Browser polyfill for module node:url …”) | move the constant into a node-free module | . | A directory declared inside another declared directory in the receiving layer | check:layout-norms (it stops qa:refresh) | move it out of the enclosing declared directory | . | A file left in BOTH layers | slice:sqlite / slice:sqlite:check (the KG export mints the same IRI twice and the slice dies on a UNIQUE constraint); node-kinds:check and kg:export do not refuse a duplicate on their own | delete the copy in the layer that no longer owns it, archived to fsh-guts/retired/ | . | Paired artefacts a move split across repositories | skills:docs (“page(s) produced by NO source”), check:declared-dirs (“absent — declared and not on disk”) | pin the receiving commits WITH the removing one (below) | . The rewrite rule . Rewrite a path only where the file exists in the destination and not in the source, and never in a record. The first half keeps a placeholder or a typo from turning into a different wrong path; the second keeps a file that moved and was later re-created from being redirected. Records say what was true when they were written, so they stay as written: proposals, todos, agent memory, work items, provenance (library figures, terminologies), upstream pins, vocab mappings, QA results and test fixtures. Generated files are rewritten by re-running their generators, never by hand. The rule is a Tool: rewrite-moved-paths (bun run cat paths:rewrite-moved --from-name <old> --from-root <dir> --to-name <new> --to-root <dir> --prefix <moved dir> … [--keep <glob>]). It reports with file and line by default, applies with --write, and with --check is the gate for a sweep that should be finished. Its test proves it never opens a proposal, a memory or a fixture. Pin the pair together, and record each consent first-hand . A move that removes files from one repository must be pinned together with the commit that adds them to the receiving one. A parent that pins the new source with the OLD pin of a receiving repository has the moved artefacts in neither, and the gates say so only indirectly. Before a re-pin, list what each new commit removes and confirm the receiving repository’s pin contains it. Every pin is a trust decision with its own consent (rule H8, remote-mount): trust.consent names who, when, the exact ref and the evidence, and mount:remote refuses a ref nobody consented to. A consent relayed by another agent is not the owner’s consent, so it is not recorded from the relay alone; record it when the owner’s answer to a question naming the exact SHAs is relayed verbatim with its time. A standing consent (“pin any main commit of these repositories that includes a fix merged in this session, listed in the PR”) covers only the repositories and the window it names, and each pin made under it is listed where the owner will read it. When a consented ref turns out not to do (a consented main with no declaration of the layer), do not substitute another ref: keep the previous pin and report it. The order that worked, and the rules for several sessions at once . | Fix the tools (the receiving layer): paths, the checks that matched paths by text, bundles, layout. | Fix the content (the source layer): prose, Tool invokes, declarations, partition rules. | Regenerate the content at matched pins, in a composed checkout laid down from the parent’s lock, to a fixed point (qa:refresh COMPLETE, then bun run cat regen, then every --check green on a fresh lay-down). | Re-pin the parent to those commits. | Run bun run cat gates on a fresh lay-down of the parent. | . When several sessions work on one separation at once: . | Hold pushes on a branch another session is superseding; hand over what is unpushed instead of racing it. | Announce which gates each session takes before starting, and re-check the open PRs and recent merges of a repository before opening one there. | Verify on the lock of the PR that will land, in a fresh scratch copy, never on another session’s checkout. | A measurement-only workaround stays local (for example a baseline entry needed to run qa:refresh while a decision is pending), is never committed, and is deleted once the real fix lands. | .

4d2f9bdb131c.title: Rollback
4d2f9bdb131c.content: Until the parent is green with the extraction declared, the extraction is additive and the parent keeps its copy; the cutover commit is the one unit worth reverting, and since the copy is ARCHIVED in the parent’s fsh-guts rather than deleted, the archive restores the exact tree that was removed. After a release, a tagged version is never reused: roll back with a new patch release and move the parent’s pin back.

7f142fb0ebe3.title: Worked examples
7f142fb0ebe3.content: 1. bootstrap + bootstrap-tools . | Stages 1–5: wrong facts, folio-only names and root-relative paths removed; graph typologies, $schema tags and QA moved out; IRIs under https://litlfred.github.io/bootstrap/ with semver. | Stage 6: bootstrap-tools/ created as a sibling; the Zod source moved down; the import cone cut to zod only; check:tools-closure and check:node-iris added, each watched failing on a planted violation. | . 2. cat-harness + the tools layer . | cat-harness (litlfred/cat-harness): owns the knowledge graph, declarative schemas, content adapters, and BPMN/DMN processes. | The tools layer: owns the MCP server (src/server.ts), concrete tool implementations (src/tools/), ambient moddle type definitions (types/), standalone package.json, tsconfig.json, and bunfig.toml. | Consumed through an index.config.json remote mount, locked in index.lock.json. The move of the harness’s remaining code into the tools layer is the case the post-move sweep was written from. | .

709620816ee6.title: Adopting a methodology, and choosing between them
709620816ee6.content: Skill methodology-adoption: How a named external methodology enters the knowledge graph, and how an agent picks which one applies. Read before following a judgement method, before adopting a new one, and before writing a house method instead of adopting one. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load . A methodology is somebody else’s work, adopted whole. It is not a house process with a citation bolted on. The graph carries them as a distinct kind so that adopting one, replacing one and removing one are all ordinary operations. Methodologies are parallel ways of achieving the same process, chosen by context; each is formalised on its own and kept independent, so that other skills can incorporate it as a sub-graph.

872943660150.title: Parallel, not composable
872943660150.content: Two or more methodologies may answer the same question. Do not blend them. A composite — this one’s vocabulary, that one’s record, a third one’s filter — is a house method that cites nobody, and it inherits none of their authority while claiming all of it. So: pick one per decision, name it, and follow it.

31ca984bf1f6.title: Choosing which applies
31ca984bf1f6.content: First: is this a judgement, or a process? . Ask before the ladder. The ladder below is about how to decide something; a request for a change is not yet a decision but work needing agreed requirements before anything is built. Sent down the ladder, it lands on the catch-all rung and produces an options analysis for a question nobody has framed yet. Is somebody asking for a change, such that requirements have to be agreed before it is built? . If yes, the question is who is asking, and does the answer depend on what a folio says? . | A change to the platform’s own capability — a tool, a schema, a pipeline, a skill, a gate — raised by somebody building the tooling, whose answer does not depend on any folio’s subject matter → the software-development process methodology. | Requirements that come from stakeholders who must sign them off, tied to a folio’s domain → the stakeholder requirements methodology. | . Both answer request → agreed requirements, so they are parallel and must not be blended — the refusal below applies to this pair first and hardest. Which is which is stated in each one’s applies-when, not here, for the reason in §”Why this skill does not name them”. If no — the change is agreed and the question is how to decide something within it — continue to the ladder. Then the ladder . Ask in this order. The first yes decides. | Do the criteria recur, with the same inputs having to produce the same answer? → the computable methodology. A one-off tabled as if it recurs asserts a repeatability it does not have. | Is the question the certainty of a body of evidence behind a recommendation? → the evidence-grading methodology. Note this is about evidence, not about a design choice that happens to be uncertain. | Is the context a work item recording a decision? → the decision-record methodology. It constrains the record, not the method, so it composes with (1) or (4) rather than competing. | Otherwise — a one-off choice among candidate options → the decision-analysis methodology. | . If none fits, that is a finding, not a licence. Say which question the decision is and that no adopted methodology covers it. Do not improvise one and do not stretch the nearest fit: either is how a house method gets in. Why this skill does not name them . Naming each methodology here would couple this skill to the set, and the set is meant to be extractable: a methodology can be lifted out, or replaced, without a prose edit here. So the declared set is the contents of the methodology graph, read from the layer’s declaration. Ask for it; do not remember it.

a3c0c9b916df.title: Node, skill, or both?
a3c0c9b916df.content: An adopted methodology can produce up to two artefacts: . | you are writing | it is a node in the methodology graph | it is a skill | . | what the method IS — its vocabulary, its constraints, what it refuses | ✅ | ❌ | . | how to PERFORM it here — the extension element, the gate, the procedure | ❌ | ✅ | . | a house process with no external origin | ❌ | ✅ — and do not dress it as an adoption | . Most adoptions produce both, and the split is the same every time: the node is the method, the skill is this platform’s application of it. The skill names the node and does not restate it, because two files carrying one definition is two copies free to drift. Three worked cases: . | raci — both. The four letters and the one-Accountable rule are the method (node); reading R from the BPMN lane, the cat-harness.processes:raci element and check:raci are this platform’s application (skill). | crdm — both (methodologies/crdm.md). PHII’s three concentration areas (Business Process Analysis, Business Process Redesign, Requirements Definition), the Business Process Matrix, swimlane Task Flow Diagrams, and PATH’s activity-linked requirement structure are the external method (node, backed by library/phii-2023-crdm, library/phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, and library/path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm); agentic facilitation, 7-dimension code impact analysis, work-item decomposition, and pull-request merge sign-off are this platform’s adaptation (crdm-requirements-workflow and crdm-requirements-template). | swot — both. | . A methodology in use with no node is invisible to the graph: check:methodology-evidence and every other reader of the methodology graph count nodes, not skills.

6d1990736f43.title: Adopting a new one — the ingestion process
6d1990736f43.content: . | Establish it is external and named. A methodology has an origin: authors, a publication, a standards body. If it has none, it is a house process — write it as a skill and do not dress it as an adoption. | Render it faithfully, and say where the rendering stops. The file carries what the method says, not a summary of what we liked. Where this platform adopts part of a method and refuses part, both halves are stated with the reason — a silent omission misrepresents the standard. | Declare its applicability. applies-when in the front matter, phrased so the selection question above can reach it, and saying what it is not for. | Place it by ownership, not by convenience. A domain-neutral method belongs to the harness; a domain method belongs to the repo that owns the domain. The separation plan decides, and the placement must make extraction literal — the directory lifts out, its declaration entry goes with it, and nothing else moves. | Declare the directory. A methodology outside a declared directory is invisible to every tool that reads the graph. | State its refusals. The part of a method a platform must not do is as load-bearing as the part it follows, and it is the part a later agent will breach first. | Ingest the source and cite it as evidence. origin names the work; evidence: library/<bib-slug> points at a copy a reader can open from this checkout. Use literature-search to find it and library-ingestion to bring it in. Where the source cannot be fetched, that is an outcome to report — a located-but-unreachable document, never a missing one — and the node keeps its origin with no evidence until somebody closes the gap. | .

9d9c027bdc9b.title: Extract the PROCESS, not the paper’s tools
9d9c027bdc9b.content: A source that presents a method through an implementation is presenting two things, and only one of them is the methodology. Render the method first, then decide which tools — existing or to be added — this platform should use to perform it. A node that adopted the source’s tool stack would be adopting an implementation and calling it a method, and it could never be falsified: the tools would work and the method would never be examined. hybrid-llm-deterministic is the worked case. Its source demonstrates the method in one tool with one model and one expression language; the node renders the rule/result inversion, the five safeguards and the bounded-truncation technique, and §”Where this rendering stops” names every tool it declined to adopt and why. The method survives replacing all of them, which is the test of whether you extracted a method at all. Ask it as: what would still be true if they had built it differently? What survives is the methodology. What does not is their engineering, and it belongs in the skill if anywhere — where this platform’s own tool choices already live. And say what the source does NOT establish. A demonstration is not an evaluation. Where a paper shows an approach working once, with no baseline and no measurement, the node records that no performance claim rests on it. Doing otherwise manufactures a finding the authors did not make — the same failure as §”Never quantify a judgement to make it look measured”, arriving through a citation instead.

bbd041ce9105.title: An origin nobody can open is not evidence
bbd041ce9105.content: A methodology’s justification is being somebody else’s named, external work, so its origin must resolve to a source a reader can open. bun run cat check:methodology-evidence is the axis that makes this visible, and test/results/methodology-evidence.qa-results.json is where it is recorded. It reports and does not gate on a missing source: whether a methodology whose source nobody can open may still be used is the owner’s call, and a gate failing on the whole corpus at once would be switched off. It does fail on front matter that does not validate, and on an evidence pointing at a bib-slug no library holds, because a citation that claims to resolve and does not is worse than none. The evidence is an input to SELECTION, not only to adoption. options-analysis.bpmn’s A_CheckEvidence reads it before the chosen methodology is applied. Adoption happens once; selection happens at every decision, and a source can stop being reachable in between. A contested origin is recorded as contested. methodologies/swot.md is the worked example: the usual attribution is repeated everywhere and its own source says no academic reference supports it, so the node declines to name an inventor: flattening that into a fact would carry the authority of a citation while resting on nothing.

5abc1518de02.title: Refusals
5abc1518de02.content: . | Never blend two methodologies into one procedure. Parallel means parallel. | Never adopt a methodology by naming it. A citation with no rendered method is an appeal to authority that no reader can check. | Never quantify a judgement to make it look measured. Where a method scores and sums, this platform adopts the structure and refuses the arithmetic: a total reads as a measurement, and the weights were invented. This is the same rule as never quoting a count from prose as though it were evidence. | Never let a rejected option go unrecorded. Whichever methodology was used, the alternatives and why they lost are part of the output — the same argument bean-coordination makes for scrapped over deleted. | Never write a method from recall and cite a paper nobody fetched. Read the source, or say you read it through another and mark each attribution second-hand. See literature-search §”Never fill the gap with recall”. | .

86f83755d7e5.title: The platform’s own gates — run what CI will run
86f83755d7e5.content: Skill platform-gates: bun test passing is not the gates passing. What to run before you push, why the list is derived from the CI workflow rather than written down, and what a *:check failure is actually telling you to do. Named by: IRIS CDN initial load, IRIS CDN nightly change ingest, IRIS CDN weekly reconciliation, Sign and publish an IRIS CDN release . One command: . bun run cat gates # the fast set bun run cat gates --all # plus the jobs that need a browser bun run cat gates:list # see them without running them . Run it before you push, not after CI tells you.

25ec434e070d.title: The CI workflow is the list
25ec434e070d.content: This skill does not list the gates, because a written list drifts from CI and a stale list reads as authoritative, so nobody checks it. bun run cat gates derives the set from .github/workflows/code-quality-gates.yml at the moment you run it, so a gate added to CI is in your next local sweep. package.json is not the authority: many of its check: scripts appear in no workflow, and running all of them would fail you on things CI does not gate. The workflow’s own comments name the scripts it deliberately excludes, with a reason beside each (for example check:ci-health is a report about main, not a gate on your diff). Read the reasons there.

3834eab11c99.title: bun test green is not the gates green
3834eab11c99.content: The test suite, tsc --noEmit and the *:check gates fail independently. One cause can also fail two gates at once. Run the gate set, not just the tests.

7a514df02afd.title: …and the gates green is not the PUBLISHED PAGE green
7a514df02afd.content: Gates read sources. A defect that exists only in a renderer’s output — for example markup that Kramdown escapes because a Liquid whitespace-strip joined two attributes — passes every gate. | Gate coverage is bounded by what a gate can look at. Ask what the gates read, not how many there are. | When your change alters a rendered page, build the page. The site build is not in the fast loop. check:escaped-markup asks one narrow version of “the output is well-formed”, and only in docs-site.yml, where _site/ exists. If the real build will not run locally (the just-the-docs remote theme 403s through the agent proxy), stub the theme and build anyway; never substitute the thing under test. continual-progress §”A template is not a page” carries the discipline. | .

4796cb7fbcd7.title: …and a green gate is not a VERIFIED FACT
4796cb7fbcd7.content: A gate can see the artefact and still answer a different question from yours. A rule that lives only in prose has a compliance ceiling nobody measures. When you write a rule into prose, ask what would fail if somebody ignored it; if the answer is nothing, you have written a wish. The measurable form is a check, a schema field, or a test. A gate’s silence is bounded by its stated scope. check:stale-paths, for example, judges two shapes — an id adjacent to an arrow, and a numbered step under a path heading — and declines everything else. Prose that merely mentions a closed work item passes it while carrying the same defect. Likewise check:ci-health labels workflow files that produced no run unjudged, not green. Green over a narrow rule is worse than red, because red is examined; a gate that does not fire is indistinguishable from one that passed. Before quoting a tick as evidence: . What does this gate say it judges, and is my claim inside it? . Read the check’s own header — every one here states its scope and its declined cases — rather than inferring the scope from the fact that it ran.

e898ed290578.title: Fast versus full is job membership
e898ed290578.content: The split is read from the workflow at run time. | fast — the typescript job. No browser. This is the inner loop. | --all — adds the jobs that install Chromium. render:bpmn:check is there because bpmn-js renders through a browser, so it can pass locally only because a browser happened to be installed. | .

1209bcaeba9c.title: Running “the gates that relate to my change” is not running the gates
1209bcaeba9c.content: Pick the gate set by JOB MEMBERSHIP, never by which gates you judge relevant. bun run cat gates --all is the whole point of there being a command. A subset chosen by an author tests the author’s model of the change, and CI tests the change; they differ precisely where the bug is. gates --all takes minutes; a red CI run costs a push cycle. A verification names a tree . A verification names a TREE, not a branch. Anything edited after the run started is unverified, however green the run was. bun run cat gates reads the WORKING TREE, not the commit. An edit made while it runs leaves the change unverified, and can make the run report failures that were never in any commit. Nothing looks wrong when this happens: the run really passed, about a different tree from the one pushed. Run the gates after the last edit, not alongside it — if you edit while they run, the run is spent and needs doing again. A skill edit is the case most likely to produce this, because a skill body has two committed artefacts generated from it. A skill edit is three files: . | file | regenerate with | . | the body, skills/<pkg>/<name>.md | — you edit it | . | test/results/kg-qa/.../<name>.kg-qa.json | bun run cat kg:audit | . | docs/reference/skill-instructions/<name>.md | bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/gen-skill-docs.ts | . The kg-qa row is a derived QA result whose record is the commit-keyed entry the CI job qa-publish stores on the orphan qa-reports branch. While a committed copy exists, kg:audit:check compares against it, so regenerate it. bun run cat skill:register does all of it in one command. A minted term needs a gloss . termIri("X") MINTS a term, and a minted term needs a gloss. Adding a new @type or a new property in kg-export.ts is therefore a TWO-file change: the emitter, and schemas/content/vocabulary.ts (CLASS_GLOSSES for a type, PROPERTY_GLOSSES for a property). ns:check refuses the half done alone. This is a different gate from the export’s own undeclared-term report: one checks that the JSON-LD @context binds the term, the other checks that the namespace DEFINES it. Both must pass, and passing the first is not evidence about the second.

6d0d00330093.title: What a *:check failure is telling you
6d0d00330093.content: Most of these gates compare a committed artefact against what its generator would produce now. A red one almost never means “the artefact is wrong”. It means you changed an input and did not regenerate. So the fix is to run the generator and commit its output — never to hand-edit the artefact into agreement, which makes the next regeneration noisy and detaches the artefact from its source. QA gates have a different shape. A gate over the qa graph computes and judges: --check writes nothing, and fails only on a finding that is NEW against a baseline — the committed working copy, or --against <ref> on the qa-reports branch. A missing baseline is UNKNOWN, printed and never a pass, never a fail. The four judge states are ok (0), finding (1), unknown and error (2) — JUDGEMENT_EXIT in scripts/qa-results.ts. A red one of THOSE is a real finding your change introduced; regenerating does not clear it, fixing the subject does. Which gates have this shape is in each script’s own docblock. Each *:check script has a generator beside it under the same stem; bun run cat gates:list shows the check, and the script it checks is named in the check’s own output when it fails.

0a2ac7d569df.title: …and a green gate set is not a CLEAN RUN
0a2ac7d569df.content: bun run cat gates snapshots the tree before the first gate and after every one, so every gate can pass and the run still exit 1: . ✗ every gate passed, and the run is NOT clean — 1 gate(s) changed the tree. The gates after the mutation were handed the repaired tree, so their verdicts describe a state you have not committed. gate-tree-mutation (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) carries the two causes, the one command that tells them apart, and the question that settles the second: does the churning field describe the subject the artefact is about, or the run that produced it? Only the first is a reason to write.

15cc610a92aa.title: Three things this skill will not do for you
15cc610a92aa.content: It does not replace reading the failure. The runner names the failing command and the CI step it belongs to, so a local failure and a red PR are findable by the same string. Read what the gate printed. It does not tell you a gate is wrong. A gate whose purpose you cannot state gets “fixed” by being made to pass, which turns the check into decoration. Every gate in that workflow carries a comment saying what it catches; if you think one is wrong, that comment is what you are arguing with. It does not make --all optional before a push that touches a diagram. Anything under processes/ changes a rendered SVG, and the check for that is in the browser job.

fef38e5137b3.title: If bun run cat gates reports no gates
fef38e5137b3.content: It fails rather than exiting clean: an empty sweep that exits 0 is indistinguishable from a passing one. If you see that refusal, the workflow was renamed or restructured and the reader needs fixing — not the gate list.

bb27a0bf3e0e.title: Related
bb27a0bf3e0e.content: |   |   | . | .github/workflows/code-quality-gates.yml | the authority, with a comment per gate saying what it catches | . | scripts/gates.ts | the reader, and the vacuity guard | . | continual-progress | commit early, open the PR at the first commit — this is the step before the push | . | prepare-merge (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) | the pre-merge recipe, which runs these plus content-type gates | . | ci-health | whether the workflows themselves are working — a different question | . | gate-tree-mutation (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc) | reading NOT clean — a green gate set over a tree a gate repaired | .
